preamble: The shift from the voiceless alveolar stop [t] to a rhotic sound [r] (specifically the alveolar tap [ɾ]) is a widespread form of lenition known as flapping. In intervocalic positions, the stop closure is shortened and voiced, resulting in a sound that is phonetically a rhotic tap.

examples.note: The /t/ is realized as a voiced tap, which is the same sound as the Spanish single 'r'.
Klingenheben's law (coronal rule): a syllable-final coronal stop becomes a rolled r
In the clipped form the t becomes syllable-final

Proto-Saharan reconstructions are Cyffer's (2020, Oxford Handbook of African Languages) as tabulated on Wikipedia. The homophonous demonstrative *tu 'that' keeps t (Kanuri túdu, Teda-Daza te̥ye), so the change is not general in initial position.
Final *t surfaces as r before an added vowel; Beria ʊ́gʊ́rī also has r.

sources: Wells, J. C. (1982). Accents of English. Cambridge University Press. https://doi.org/10.1017/CBO9780511611759
Newman, P. (2004). Klingenheben's Law in Hausa. Rüdiger Köppe. https://lccn.loc.gov/2005390185
